questions.question: How do you reverse a String in Java?
questions.title: Reverse a String
questions.direct_answer: Use StringBuilder's reverse() method for simplicity and performance, or manually iterate the string backwards building a new string. StringBuilder is preferred because it's mutable and avoids creating multiple intermediate String objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of String immutability and knowledge of StringBuilder as the proper tool for string manipulation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to modify a String in place (impossible due to immutability) or using inefficient string concatenation in a loop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate both the StringBuilder approach and manual iteration, explain why StringBuilder is O(n) while string concatenation would be O(n²), and mention when you'd use each

sections.title: String Reversal Fundamentals
sections.content: Reversing a string is a fundamental operation in text processing, from validating palindromes to parsing user input in reverse order. In Java, **String objects are immutable** — once created, their content cannot change. This means you can't reverse a String in place. Instead, you need a **mutable structure** like **StringBuilder** or build a new String from scratch. Think of it like reordering printed pages: you can't erase and rewrite the original paper, so you either use a whiteboard (StringBuilder) where you can rearrange freely, or you print new pages in reverse order. The **StringBuilder.reverse()** method is the industry-standard approach — it's a single method call, runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space (reverses in place within the StringBuilder's internal character array), and is optimized by the JVM. Manual reversal gives you more control and helps interviewers assess your loop logic and edge-case handling.

sections.title: String Reversal Using StringBuilder and Manual Iteration
Key Points
content: **String immutability**: Strings cannot be modified after creation, so reversal requires creating a new String or using a mutable builder
**StringBuilder.reverse()**: Single method call, O(n) time, O(1) extra space, reverses the internal char array in place — this is the production approach
**Manual iteration**: Start from input.length() - 1 and decrement to 0, appending each character to a StringBuilder — useful for custom logic or interview demonstrations
**Edge cases**: Always check for null and empty strings before processing to avoid NullPointerException or unnecessary work
**Performance**: StringBuilder reversal is O(n), manual with StringBuilder is also O(n), but string concatenation (using +) would be O(n²) due to repeated String object creation
**Use cases**: Palindrome checking (compare string with its reverse), parsing tokens in reverse order, or generating mirrored output for reports
**Interview insight**: Showing both approaches demonstrates you know the optimal tool (StringBuilder) but also understand the underlying algorithm

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd reverse a String using StringBuilder's reverse method. Here's why that's the go-to approach. Since Strings are immutable in Java, you can't change them in place. So I create a new StringBuilder from the input string and call its reverse method, then convert back to String with toString. This takes O of n time and runs fast because StringBuilder uses a mutable character array internally. For example, if I have the string Java Developer, I'd do new StringBuilder in parens Java Developer close parens dot reverse dot toString, and I get repoleveD avaJ. Now, if the interviewer wants to see the manual approach, I'd iterate backwards through the original string using a for loop. Start at input dot length minus one, go down to zero, and append each character to a fresh StringBuilder. That also takes O of n time and shows I understand the loop logic. One common mistake is trying to use string concatenation with the plus operator in a loop. That's O of n squared because each concatenation creates a new String object. You'd only do manual iteration if you need custom logic, like skipping certain characters while reversing. Otherwise, StringBuilder dot reverse is cleaner and what you'd use in production code.

questions.question: How do you count the frequency of each character in a String?
questions.title: Character Frequency Count
questions.direct_answer: Use a HashMap with Character keys and Integer values to store frequencies. Iterate through the string, and for each character, increment its count using getOrDefault or merge. For only lowercase English letters, an int array of size 26 is more space-efficient.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to use HashMap for frequency counting and understanding of when an array solution is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a primitive array without considering Unicode or special characters, or writing verbose HashMap updates instead of using getOrDefault or merge
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both HashMap and array approaches, explain time-space trade-offs, and extend to finding the first non-repeating character using the same frequency map

sections.title: Character Frequency Counting Approaches
sections.content: Counting character frequencies is essential for text analysis tasks like finding duplicates, validating input constraints, or identifying the first unique character in a stream. The core idea is to **scan the string once** and maintain a count for each character encountered. You have two main options: a **HashMap<Character, Integer>** which works for any Unicode character and is flexible, or an **int array** (like int[26] for lowercase letters) which is faster and uses less memory but only works for a known fixed character set. Think of the HashMap as a general-purpose filing cabinet where you can store any character and its count, while the array is like a pre-labeled shelf with exactly 26 slots for a-z. The **HashMap approach** uses O(n) time for iteration and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters. The **array approach** is O(n) time and O(1) space when the character set size is constant. Modern Java provides **getOrDefault** and **merge** methods on Map to make frequency updates concise and readable.

sections.title: Character Frequency Counting with HashMap and Array
Key Points
content: **HashMap approach**: Use HashMap<Character, Integer> with merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) to increment counts cleanly — works for any Unicode character including spaces and punctuation
**Array approach**: Use int[26] for lowercase letters, mapping each character c to index c minus a — O(1) space but limited to a fixed character set like ASCII lowercase
**merge method**: map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) either inserts 1 if key is absent or applies Integer::sum to the existing value and 1 — cleaner than getOrDefault
**getOrDefault alternative**: map.put(c, map.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1) is more verbose but equally valid if merge feels unfamiliar
**Time complexity**: Both approaches are O(n) where n is string length — you iterate once through the input
**Space complexity**: HashMap uses O(k) space where k is distinct characters (up to 65536 for all Unicode), array is O(1) for fixed-size alphabets
**Extended use case**: Once you have the frequency map, you can find the first non-repeating character by scanning the string again and checking if map.get(c) equals 1

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To count character frequencies, I'd use a HashMap with Character as the key and Integer as the value. I iterate through the string using toCharArray, and for each character, I call the merge method on the map. The merge method is really handy here. I pass the character, the number one, and Integer colon colon sum. What that does is if the character is already in the map, it adds one to the existing count. If it's not there yet, it inserts one. So after one pass through the string, I have a complete frequency map. For example, if the input is success, the map would show s maps to three, u maps to one, c maps to two, e maps to one. That's an O of n operation where n is the string length. Now, if the problem says we're only dealing with lowercase English letters, I'd use an int array of size twenty-six instead. It's faster and uses constant space. I'd iterate the string, convert each character to lowercase if needed, then increment the array at index c minus the letter a. So for the letter c, that's index two. One common mistake freshers make is using a basic array without checking the character range, which can cause an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException if there are numbers or punctuation. The HashMap is safer for general input. If the follow-up question is to find the first non-repeating character, I'd use the same frequency map and scan the original string again, returning the first character where the count equals one.

questions.question: How do you check if two Strings are anagrams?
questions.title: Anagram Check
questions.direct_answer: Two approaches: sort both strings using toCharArray and Arrays.sort, then compare with Arrays.equals; or count character frequencies in one string and decrement for the other, checking if all counts are zero. Both are O(n log n) for sorting and O(n) for frequency counting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Algorithm design skills and understanding of multiple solution approaches with trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not checking if lengths are equal first (fast rejection for non-anagrams), or ignoring case sensitivity and whitespace in user input
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Present both the sorting and frequency-counting solutions, analyze their time complexities, and explain when each is preferable — sorting is simpler code, frequency is faster for large character sets

sections.title: Anagram Detection Strategies
sections.content: An **anagram** is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another word, using each original character exactly once. For example, listen and silent are anagrams. This problem appears in text processing, game development (word games like Scrabble), and validation of user-generated content. The key insight is that two strings are anagrams if and only if they contain the **same characters with the same frequencies**. You can verify this in two ways: **sorting** both strings and comparing them character by character, or **counting character frequencies** in both strings and ensuring they match. Think of sorting like organizing two decks of letter cards alphabetically — if the sorted decks are identical, the original decks had the same letters. The frequency approach is like having two bags of letters and verifying each bag has the same count of each letter type. **Sorting** is simpler to code (3-4 lines) and runs in O(n log n) time. **Frequency counting** is O(n) time but requires more code and O(k) space for the frequency map where k is distinct characters.

sections.title: Anagram Detection Using Sorting and Frequency Counting
Key Points
content: **Length check first**: If strings have different lengths, they can't be anagrams — return false immediately without further processing
**Sorting approach**: Convert both strings to char arrays, sort them with Arrays.sort, then compare with Arrays.equals — simple and O(n log n) time complexity
**Frequency approach**: Count characters in the first string (increment), then process the second string (decrement) — if the map is empty at the end, they're anagrams
**Case sensitivity**: Always normalize to lowercase or uppercase before comparison unless the problem explicitly requires case-sensitive anagrams
**Space complexity**: Sorting is O(1) extra space if you exclude the char arrays, frequency counting is O(k) where k is distinct characters
**Performance**: Frequency counting is faster at O(n) but requires more code — sorting is O(n log n) but only takes 4 lines and is easier to read
**Whitespace handling**: For real user input like the strings listen and silent with spaces, use replaceAll to remove spaces before checking: s.replaceAll whitespace-regex empty-string

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd check if two strings are anagrams by first comparing their lengths. If they're different, they can't be anagrams, so I return false right away. That's an early exit optimization. Then I have two approaches I can use. The simpler one is sorting. I convert both strings to lowercase, then to char arrays, sort each array using Arrays dot sort, and compare them with Arrays dot equals. If the sorted arrays are identical, the original strings are anagrams. For example, listen becomes e-i-l-n-s-t and silent also becomes e-i-l-n-s-t, so they match. This approach is O of n log n because of the sorting step, and the code is really clean — just four or five lines. The second approach is frequency counting, which is faster at O of n. I use a HashMap to count each character in the first string, incrementing counts. Then I iterate through the second string and decrement the counts. At the end, if the HashMap is empty, meaning all counts went to zero, the strings are anagrams. This approach is better for very long strings because it avoids the log n factor. One mistake I'd avoid is forgetting to handle case sensitivity. I always convert to lowercase first unless the problem says otherwise. Another mistake is not checking lengths upfront — that wastes time sorting or counting when you could reject immediately. In an interview, I'd present both solutions and say the sorting approach is what I'd write quickly in production because it's simpler, but if performance matters for huge strings, I'd use frequency counting.

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a String?
questions.title: First Non-Repeating Character
questions.direct_answer: Use a two-pass algorithm: first pass builds a HashMap of character frequencies, second pass scans the original string and returns the first character with count equal to 1. This preserves insertion order and runs in O(n) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of two-pass algorithms and HashMap usage for frequency tracking while preserving order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Attempting a complex one-pass solution with unnecessary data structures when two simple passes are cleaner and still linear time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the int[26] array optimization for lowercase-only input (O(1) space), and briefly explain the LinkedHashMap or Stream-based queue approach as advanced alternatives

sections.title: Finding the First Non-Repeating Character
sections.content: Finding the first non-repeating character is a classic problem in stream processing, text analysis, and interview coding challenges. The goal is to scan a string and return the **first character that appears exactly once**, preserving the order in which characters appear. For example, in the string success, the first non-repeating character is u. The key challenge is that you need **both frequency information and insertion order**. You can't determine if a character is unique until you've seen the entire string, but you need to remember which unique character came first. The **two-pass approach** is the standard solution: in the **first pass**, count character frequencies using a **HashMap<Character, Integer>**; in the **second pass**, iterate the original string and return the first character whose frequency is 1. This is O(n) time because each pass is linear, and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters. Think of it like reading a guest list twice: first time you tally how many times each name appears, second time you walk down the original list and announce the first person who came alone.

sections.title: First Non-Repeating Character with HashMap Two-Pass
Key Points
content: **Two-pass algorithm**: First pass counts frequencies in a HashMap, second pass scans the original string and returns the first character with count 1 — simple and O(n) time
**Order preservation**: The second pass uses the original string (not the HashMap keySet) to preserve insertion order — HashMap iteration order is not guaranteed
**Frequency map**: Use HashMap<Character, Integer> with merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) for clean frequency counting in the first pass
**Array optimization**: For lowercase ASCII only, use int[26] instead of HashMap — O(1) space and faster lookups, map character c to index c minus a
**Return type**: Return Character (nullable object) instead of char primitive so you can return null when no non-repeating character exists
**Edge cases**: Handle null input and empty string by returning null immediately — also consider strings where all characters repeat

**Advanced alternative**: LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order in keySet, allowing a single-pass frequency count followed by iteration over the map entries, but two passes on the string is clearer for interviews

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd find the first non-repeating character using a two-pass approach with a HashMap. Here's how it works. In the first pass, I iterate through the string and build a frequency map. For each character, I use the merge method to increment its count, just like we did for character frequency counting. So after the first pass, I know how many times each character appears. Then in the second pass, I iterate through the original string again — not the HashMap, but the actual string to preserve order — and I check the frequency map for each character. The first character I encounter with a count of one is the answer, and I return it immediately. For example, in the string success, the frequency map shows s appears three times, u appears once, c appears twice, and e appears once. When I scan the original string in the second pass, I see s first but it has count three, then u with count one, so I return u. That's the first non-repeating character. This approach is O of n time because both passes are linear, and O of k space where k is the number of distinct characters. One mistake freshers make is trying to solve this in one pass with complex logic. Two passes is cleaner and still linear time, so it's perfectly efficient. If the interviewer asks for an optimization, I'd mention that if the input is guaranteed to be lowercase English letters only, I can use an int array of size twenty-six instead of a HashMap. That's O of one space and faster lookups. The algorithm stays the same — two passes, one to count and one to find. This problem is common in stream processing where you're reading user input or log files and need to identify unique events in order.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicate characters from a String preserving order?
questions.title: Remove Duplicate Characters
questions.direct_answer: Use a LinkedHashSet which maintains insertion order and automatically rejects duplicates. Add each character to the set, then collect the set contents back into a String. This is O(n) time and preserves the original order of first occurrence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of LinkedHashSet's unique property of combining Set behavior with insertion-order preservation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a regular HashSet which loses order, or using StringBuilder with contains() which works but is O(n²) for large strings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the LinkedHashSet solution, explain why HashSet fails, and discuss the StringBuilder alternative with its performance trade-off — demonstrates awareness of data structure properties

sections.title: Removing Duplicates While Preserving Order
sections.content: Removing duplicate characters while preserving the original order is a common requirement in text sanitization, generating unique tokens, or processing user input where you want to keep only the first occurrence of each character. The challenge is that you need **both uniqueness and order** — a regular **HashSet** gives you uniqueness but loses insertion order, while a **List** preserves order but allows duplicates. The solution is **LinkedHashSet**, a Java collection that combines the best of both worlds: it rejects duplicate elements like a Set, and maintains **insertion order** like a List using an internal doubly-linked list. Think of it as a membership club that remembers the order people joined — if someone tries to join twice, you ignore the second attempt but remember when they first joined. The algorithm is simple: iterate through the string, add each character to a LinkedHashSet (duplicates are silently rejected), then collect the set back into a String. This runs in **O(n) time** because add and contains operations on LinkedHashSet are O(1) on average, and **O(k) space** where k is the number of distinct characters.

sections.title: Removing Duplicates with LinkedHashSet and StringBuilder
Key Points
content: **LinkedHashSet**: Maintains insertion order and rejects duplicates automatically — perfect for this problem, add operation is O(1) on average
**Why not HashSet**: Regular HashSet does not preserve insertion order — using it would give you unique characters but in an arbitrary order
**Collecting back**: Convert LinkedHashSet to String by streaming, mapping each Character to String, and joining — or iterate and append to StringBuilder
**StringBuilder alternative**: Iterate the string, check if character is already in result with indexOf, and append if not — works but indexOf is O(n) making total complexity O(n²)
**Performance trade-off**: LinkedHashSet is O(n) time and O(k) space (k distinct chars), StringBuilder approach is O(n²) time but O(k) space — LinkedHashSet wins for large strings
**Stream approach**: uniqueChars.stream().map(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining()) is functional style — clear intent but slightly more verbose than a loop
**Use case**: Sanitizing user IDs by removing repeated characters, generating unique character sets for game word validation, or cleaning noisy text input

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To remove duplicate characters while keeping the original order, I'd use a LinkedHashSet. Here's why that's the right tool. A LinkedHashSet is a Set, so it automatically rejects duplicates when you try to add the same element twice. But unlike a regular HashSet, it also maintains insertion order using an internal linked list. So I iterate through the input string, and for each character, I add it to the LinkedHashSet. If it's already there, the add operation does nothing, which is perfect. Then I convert the set back to a String by streaming over it, mapping each Character to a String, and collecting with Collectors dot joining. For example, if the input is programming, the first p goes in, then r, then o, then g, then r again but it's rejected, then a, then m, then m rejected, then i, then n, then g rejected. The final set is p-r-o-g-a-m-i-n in that order, so the result is progamin. This runs in O of n time because adding to a LinkedHashSet is O of one on average, and O of k space where k is the number of distinct characters. Now, if I didn't know about LinkedHashSet, I could use a StringBuilder and manually check if each character is already present using indexOf before appending. That works and the code is simple, but it's O of n squared because indexOf scans the StringBuilder each time. For short strings that's fine, but for long inputs, LinkedHashSet is much faster. One common mistake is using a regular HashSet thinking it'll work, but you lose order, so the output characters are jumbled. In an interview, I'd lead with LinkedHashSet, mention the StringBuilder alternative and its performance downside, and explain when each is appropriate. That shows I know data structure properties and can reason about trade-offs.
